fields.mechanism: Biofilm formation on catheter surfaces that provides a scaffold for microbial colonization and thrombus development.
fields.intervention: Apply a dual‑function coating that continuously releases nitric oxide (NO) to chemically inhibit biofilm formation while presenting a hydrophilic, anti‑protein surface to block heparin‑binding thrombus.
fields.expected_effect: Reduced biofilm accumulation diminishes the extracellular matrix that traps platelets and fibrin; NO also suppresses platelet activation, together preserving long‑term catheter patency.
fields.falsification_test: In a controlled in‑vitro flow loop with heparin‑treated blood, compare biofilm biomass (crystal violet assay) and thrombus mass (gravimetric measurement) on NO‑releasing coated catheters versus uncoated controls over a 7‑day period.

fields.mechanism: Biofilm formation on catheter surfaces provides a scaffold that promotes heparin‑binding thrombus accumulation.
fields.intervention: Apply an anti‑biofilm polymer coating (e.g., surface‑bound antimicrobial peptide or quorum‑sensing inhibitor) to the luminal surface of the tunneled hemodialysis catheter, replacing the existing antithrombotic coating.
fields.expected_effect: Inhibition of microbial adhesion and extracellular polymer matrix development will reduce protein and platelet adhesion, thereby decreasing heparin‑binding thrombus formation and extending long‑term catheter patency.
fields.falsification_test: Perform an in‑vitro dialysis flow loop comparing standard heparin‑binding coated catheters to catheters with the anti‑biofilm coating, quantifying thrombus mass and heparin‑binding protein deposition after 72 hours of simulated use.
